abstract: Background Shared intense experiences are thought to bring people closer, and synchronized physiology is a proposed reason. We examined heart rate and synchrony across ride phases, riders' response profiles, and whether these relate to changes in happiness, stress and closeness. Methods In this exploratory field study we recorded heart rate in 439 riders (418 with usable data) on 19 trains of the Balder roller coaster, Gothenburg, Sweden, and measured happiness, stress and closeness (0-10) just before and after the ride. Real pairs were compared with surrogate pairs from different trains, aligned on ride start, to separate coupling between riders from the ride's own effect. Profiles came from k-means clustering; analyses used linear mixed models. Results Heart rate rose by 15.2 beats per minute (95% CI 14.2 to 16.3) during the two-minute ride and was back at baseline within nine minutes. Heart-rate curves did not form clearly distinct types (two profiles, silhouette 0.29): riders calm in the queue rose more and stayed elevated, while riders already aroused rose less. Pairs in which both riders came with companions gained more synchrony during the ride than the surrogate benchmark (Fisher z 0.096, 95% CI 0.050 to 0.142); for pairs including a solo rider the boost was smaller and uncertain. This coupling peaked just after the ride and was gone five minutes later. Riders reported being happier (+1.3 points, Cohen's d = 0.87) and closer to the other riders on the train (+2.2 points, d = 0.70). Neither phase-specific heart-rate responses, response profile nor synchrony was associated with these changes. Conclusions A short shared thrill coupled riders' heart rates beyond what the ride alone explains, and riders felt happier and closer to others on the train afterwards, but the two ran in parallel. Without a non-riding comparison, the psychological changes cannot be attributed to the ride itself.
